people/charles-finney/summary: Lawyer turned revivalist in upstate New York's 'burned-over district' who introduced 'new measures' such as the anxious bench and protracted meetings, teaching that revival is the right use of means. As president of Oberlin College he promoted abolition, coeducation and perfectionism.
people/charles-finney/keyIdeas/2: Social reform as fruit of conversion
people/charles-hodge/summary: Professor at Princeton Theological Seminary for over fifty years, whose Systematic Theology championed Reformed confessional orthodoxy and the inspiration of Scripture. He criticised Darwinism as atheistic where it excluded design, and contributed to the Princeton doctrine of inerrancy.
people/john-nelson-darby/summary: Anglo-Irish former Anglican priest, a founder of the Plymouth Brethren. He developed dispensationalism, distinguishing Israel from the church and teaching a secret pre-tribulation rapture; his ideas spread through Bible conferences and later the Scofield Reference Bible.
people/john-mcleod-campbell/summary: Church of Scotland minister deposed in 1831 for teaching that Christ died for all and that believers may have assurance. His The Nature of the Atonement (1856) presents Christ's 'vicarious repentance' — a perfect confession of the Father's judgement on sin — and influenced the Torrances.
people/joseph-smith/summary: Founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, who reported visions of God the Father and Jesus (1820) and an angel guiding him to golden plates he published as the Book of Mormon (1830). He led his followers from New York to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, introduced temple rites and plural marriage, and was killed by a mob at Carthage jail. His movement stands outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
people/joseph-smith/keyIdeas/0: Restoration of the church through new revelation
people/phoebe-palmer/summary: Methodist laywoman whose Tuesday Meeting for the Promotion of Holiness in New York and book The Way of Holiness taught an 'altar theology' of instantaneous entire sanctification by consecration and faith. She preached widely and defended women's ministry in Promise of the Father.
people/samuel-ajayi-crowther/summary: A Yoruba boy enslaved in 1821 and freed by the Royal Navy, educated in Freetown, who became the first African Anglican bishop (1864) in charge of the Niger Mission. He translated the Bible into Yoruba and compiled grammars of several languages; European missionaries' undermining of his authority before his death became a turning point for African church independence.
people/andrew-kim-taegon/summary: The first Korean-born Catholic priest, trained in Macau and ordained in Shanghai in 1845. Arrested while arranging missionary entry by sea, he was beheaded at Saenamteo near Seoul aged 25; he is the patron of Korean clergy, canonised with 102 companions in 1984.
people/ellen-g-white/summary: A Millerite who reported some 2,000 visions after 1844 and co-founded the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863). Adventists regard her as a messenger with the gift of prophecy, subordinate to Scripture; her writings shaped Sabbath observance, health reform and education. Critics question her claims and borrowings from other authors.
people/ellen-g-white/keyIdeas/3: Great controversy between Christ and Satan
people/hudson-taylor/summary: Yorkshire-born missionary to China who founded the China Inland Mission (1865), sending interdenominational missionaries — including many single women — into all of China's interior provinces. He adopted Chinese dress and pioneered the 'faith mission' model of trusting God for support.
people/charles-spurgeon/summary: Baptist pastor of London's Metropolitan Tabernacle, the most popular preacher of Victorian England, whose sermons were printed weekly and sold worldwide. A Calvinist evangelist, he founded a college and orphanage and left the Baptist Union during the Downgrade controversy (1887).
people/cyrus-scofield/summary: Lawyer and Congregational minister in Dallas whose Scofield Reference Bible (1909, rev. 1917) set dispensational premillennialism in its notes. It became the most influential study Bible among American fundamentalists.
people/charles-taze-russell/summary: Pittsburgh businessman influenced by Adventist teachers who founded the Bible Student movement and Zion's Watch Tower (1879). He rejected the Trinity and eternal torment and predicted the end of the Gentile Times in 1914. Jehovah's Witnesses, organised after him, stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
people/charles-taze-russell/keyIdeas/0: Rejection of the Trinity and hellfire
people/william-wade-harris/summary: A Liberian Grebo teacher and former Methodist and Episcopal worker who, after a vision in prison in 1910, walked along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast (1913–15) as a prophet in white robes. He baptised perhaps 120,000 people, the largest mass movement in West African history, before French expulsion.
people/walter-rauschenbusch/summary: German-American Baptist pastor in New York's 'Hell's Kitchen' and Rochester seminary professor, the leading voice of the Social Gospel. Christianity and the Social Crisis and A Theology for the Social Gospel called churches to work for the Kingdom of God in economic and social structures.
people/walter-rauschenbusch/keyIdeas/0: Kingdom of God as social transformation
people/uchimura-kanzo/summary: Japanese Christian writer converted at Sapporo Agricultural College, who refused to bow before the Imperial Rescript on Education (1891). He founded the Mukyōkai ('Non-Church') movement of Bible study without clergy or sacraments, seeking a Christianity rooted in Japanese soil.
people/tikhon-of-moscow/summary: Bishop for North America (1898–1907), where he helped organise Orthodoxy among immigrants, then elected Patriarch of Moscow in 1917. He anathematised Bolshevik violence, was imprisoned and pressured by the Soviet state and died in 1925; he was canonised in 1989.
people/isaiah-shembe/summary: Zulu healer and prophet who founded the amaNazaretha (Nazareth Baptist Church) in 1910, with a holy city at Ekuphakameni and pilgrimage to the mountain Nhlangakazi. His hymns blend biblical faith with Zulu culture; his followers venerate him as a prophet sent to Africa.
people/william-j-seymour/summary: Son of formerly enslaved parents in Louisiana, a Holiness preacher blind in one eye who accepted Parham's teaching on tongues. As pastor of the Apostolic Faith Mission on Azusa Street from 1906 he led the interracial revival that launched worldwide Pentecostalism; he later emphasised love and unity over tongues as the evidence of the Spirit.
people/william-j-seymour/keyIdeas/2: Love as evidence of the Spirit
people/charles-parham/summary: Holiness preacher whose Bethel Bible School in Topeka saw Agnes Ozman speak in tongues on 1 January 1901. He formulated the doctrine that tongues are the initial evidence of Spirit baptism and taught Seymour in Houston, but rejected Azusa's interracial worship and later supported segregation; a 1907 scandal diminished his influence.
people/v-s-azariah/summary: Tamil evangelist who founded the Indian Missionary Society and became the first Indian Anglican bishop (Dornakal, 1912). He led mass movements among Dalit communities in Telugu country, pleaded at Edinburgh 1910 for true friendship between missionaries and Indian Christians, and worked for the union that produced the Church of South India.
people/evan-roberts/summary: Former coal miner and ministerial student whose meetings in Loughor in late 1904 sparked the Welsh Revival. His four-point call — confess sin, remove doubtful things, obey the Spirit promptly, confess Christ publicly — spread across Wales; after a breakdown he withdrew into private prayer for decades.
people/gustaf-aulen/summary: Swedish Lutheran theologian of the Lund school and bishop of Strängnäs, whose Christus Victor (1931) argued that the 'classic' patristic and Lutheran view of the atonement is Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil, distinct from Latin satisfaction and liberal moral-influence theories.
people/john-xxiii/summary: Angelo Roncalli, papal diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and France and patriarch of Venice, elected pope in 1958 as a caretaker. He surprised the world by calling the Second Vatican Council for aggiornamento and wrote Pacem in Terris on peace and human rights; he was canonised in 2014.
people/rudolf-bultmann/summary: Marburg New Testament scholar who pioneered form criticism and called for 'demythologising' the New Testament — interpreting its mythic world-picture existentially as a call to authentic faith. Influential and contested, he was also a member of the Confessing Church.
people/karl-barth/summary: Swiss Reformed pastor whose commentary on Romans (1919) broke with liberal theology, insisting on God's sovereign self-revelation in Jesus Christ. Principal author of the Barmen Declaration, expelled from Germany in 1935, he wrote the vast Church Dogmatics, recasting election as God's choice of humanity in Christ.
people/karl-barth/keyIdeas/2: Word of God in threefold form
